structured_output.hypothesis: In sunflower capitula, the angles at which the two families of contact parastichy spirals cross are roughly constant across the disc (isogonal) at a value that is not 90 degrees in most heads, so orthogonal crossing is the exception.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Using per-floret centre coordinates from at least 30 capitula, compute the crossing angle of the two nearest-neighbour parastichy families in each head. The claim passes if (a) in at least 80% of heads the within-head spread of crossing angle between radial annuli is under 10 degrees (standard deviation), and (b) fewer than 25% of heads have a mean crossing angle within 5 degrees of 90 degrees.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The claim fails if the within-head crossing angle varies by 10 degrees or more (standard deviation) in more than 50% of heads, or if 50% or more of heads have a mean crossing angle within 5 degrees of 90 degrees.
structured_output.interpretation: Thompson's 'spirals' are the contact parastichies, i.e. the visible left- and right-handed spiral families. 'Isogonal' means a constant crossing angle, as in logarithmic spirals about a common pole. 'Orthogonal' means a 90 degree crossing, which Church had argued for. The modern quantity is the angle between the local parastichy directions, computed from floret or seed centre coordinates by Delaunay or nearest-neighbour lattice vectors. Real sunflower heads follow a Vogel-type lattice, so the crossing angle may drift with radius. That drift is what the (a) threshold tests. Orthogonality is expected near the rim of Fibonacci-type heads and not elsewhere.
structured_output.no_dataset_reason: I could not find a public dataset with a verified landing page or DOI that records per-floret centre coordinates or parastichy crossing angles for sunflower capitula. A search of the open portals found only related items. Swinton's arXiv paper 2407.05857 (Disk-stacking models are consistent with Fibonacci and non-Fibonacci structure in sunflowers) refers to a large dataset of seedheads, but its arXiv page gives no repository, no dataset DOI and no URL, and it describes parastichy counts rather than coordinates or angles. Parastichy counts alone cannot decide a test about crossing angles. The capitulum-inclination record on data.gov is about head tilt, not floret positions. Naming any of these as the dataset would misrepresent it, and I will not guess at a supplement from memory. The test needs a new set of sunflower head images with floret centres extracted, or a published coordinate set that I have not verified.
